Hubble Space Telescope Servicing Missions. Hubble launched on April 24, 1990, but something was terribly wrong. The primary mirror was flawed, and instead of the sharp images it was designed to produce, Hubble gave blurred pictures. It was a devastating flaw in what was meant to be humanity's premier space observatory. But the problem had a solution.

The first servicing mission launched on December 2, 1993, carrying a corrective optics module called COSTAR and new instruments that compensated for the mirror defect. Astronauts performed spacewalks to install the repair hardware and new instruments during the mission, demonstrating the value of human spaceflight for complex maintenance tasks that no robot could accomplish as effectively.

Subsequent servicing missions followed in 1997, 1999, 2002, and 2009. These upgraded Hubble's instruments, replaced solar panels, batteries, and gyroscopes, and extended its operational life well beyond its original design. The final servicing mission in May 2009 was one of the most dangerous Space Shuttle missions ever flown, as the shuttle had to boost Hubble's orbit to a safe altitude while servicing it. The repairs and upgrades paid off handsomely. Hubble discovered dark energy, revealed the universe's age and expansion rate, imaged deep fields containing thousands of galaxies, and captured images of exoplanet atmospheres. The Hubble Space Telescope Servicing Missions remain exemplars of human spaceflight's unique value for on-orbit repair and adaptation of complex machinery.
